_note: The Fiddle in the Woods (decision 0427): the main story's fourth chapter, from the Bark Road to the switchbacks down to Harlow Bridge. The beat is docs/regions/tanbark-road.md, 'The main beat'. Draft lines, for Matt or his writer friend. src/story/fiddle.ts stages the night walk and the far figure.

lines.text: A bull moose stands square in the middle of the road, as tall at the shoulder as a horse, and broader. His antlers are a yard across.
He looks at Eldwin's staff, lowers his head, and paws the ground.
He thinks that stick's a rival. I'd put it behind you.
The bull wrenches his antlers free of the beech, bellows once at the whole wood, and crashes off into the trees.
They hear him a long way off, still bellowing.
Well. He'll be telling everyone about that.
Under a big hemlock, a camp. A kettle has just come to the boil.
You came the long way. You always do.
It's the only way down.
So it is. Tea's on. The fire's on account.
Dark comes early under these trees. Sit, if you're stopping.
That's ours, that wall. My great-grandfather's, maybe further. Look at the batter on it.
It's held a long time.
It'll hold longer.
That tune. You played it, on the Post Road.
Old song. Everybody's got a verse of it somewhere.
He doesn't say which verse he has.
The fire burns down. Jasper banks it. The hemlocks close in, and the cold comes off the wall.
Mrs. Applegate won't settle. She stands with her head up, facing along the wall.
Eldwin sleeps.
He wakes in the dark. The fire is embers.
Far off along the wall, a fiddle. The tune he knows from Jasper's fire on the Post Road.
He plays most nights. He won't thank you for following.
Jasper is awake, looking into the fire. He doesn't look up.
Then, back in the hemlocks the other way, a scream. High and long, like a woman's.
And that's the cat. Everybody says they're gone from these woods.
Is it coming here?
It's been round the fire twice already. You'll not hit what you can't see.
Give it no opening. All of you braced at once, and it can't stand not knowing. It comes out to look.
The worn place on the wall, where the moss is gone from the top stones. Nobody.
A cider jug, stoppered, set down on the wall. It's still warm from a hand.
Boot prints in the frost, going off along the wall toward the valley.
A last few notes, further off. Then nothing.
Told you.
You did.
Jasper puts another stick on the fire and says nothing else until morning.
First light. The valley opens below.
Far down the switchbacks, a tall, stooped figure is walking into town, a fiddle under his arm.
Too far to call to.
A tin cup on a nail over the spring. Dented. Full to the brim, though nobody's been by since dark.
Inside the hollow chestnut, cut low in the wood where a child could reach: H.B.
The letters are years old. The edges have gone soft.
The moss is gone from these few stones, worn off, as if someone sits here often.
A stone bench at the top of the ledge, where the whole valley shows.
Cut into the seat, joined by a plus: T.B. and M.B. Under them, the date of a wedding.
Chalk tallies on every rick end, in the same round hand. The latest says forty-five.
A bark sled with one runner gone. Somebody meant to mend it.
A sack of beechnuts with a red string round its neck, dropped in the leaves. Something has been at one corner.
The tin cup over the spring is empty this morning, for the first time. Whoever drinks from it has gone on down the hill.
It comes off the nail easily, as if it had been waiting.
A bull moose stands square in the middle of the road, as tall at the shoulder as a horse, and broader. His antlers are a yard across.
He looks at Eldwin's staff, lowers his head, and paws the ground.
He thinks that stick's a rival. I'd put it behind you.
